APPELLANT'S STATED ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR
I. The Trial Court erred by denying Appellant default Judgment, by abuse of discretion by relying on clearly erroneous findings of facts.
II. The Trial Court erred in granting Appellee's Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgments [issue or claim preclusion) that covers up past judicial litigant collusion, in Case CV04 547780 which is forbidden by law.
Appellee, Deutsche Bank Trust Company America f/k/a Bankers Trust Company, as Trustee ("Appellee"), does not believe the Trial Court erred in denying Appellant's Motion for Default Judgment or granting Appellee's Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment and, therefore, the judgment of the Trial Court should be affirmed.
ISSUES PRESENTED FOR REVIEW
A. WHETHER THE TRIAL COURT ABUSED ITS DISCRETION IN DENYING APPELLANT'S MOTION FOR DEFAULT JUDGMENT.
B. WHETHER THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING APPELLEE'S MOTION TO DISMISS OR, IN THE ALTERNATIVE, MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
This action arises out of a Complaint filed on November 30, 2007. On January 10, 2008, Appellee filed a Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment. The same day, Appellant filed a Motion for Default Judgment. On January 15, 2008, Appellee filed its Response to Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment. The Motion for Default Judgment was subsequently denied on January 18, 2008.
-

Following the completion of briefing regarding Appellee's Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment, the Trial Court granted Appellee's Motion, finding that Appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law. This appeal timely followed.
FACTS
This case arises out of a prior foreclosure action filed by Deutsche Bank in the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas. On November 17, 2004, Deutsche Bank filed a Complaint in Foreclosure and for Reformation of Mortgage in the Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas. The case was assigned to the Honorable Kathleen A. Sutula, bearing Case No. CV-04-547780. (R. at Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment ("Motion to Dismiss"), Exhibit "A").
As set forth in the foreclosure Complaint, Deutsche Bank was the holder and owner of a Note executed by Jacqueline Barksdale-Williams ("Barksdale-Williams") and Perry Williams a/k/a Perry Williams, Jr. ("Williams"). (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "A"). The Note was secured by a Mortgage, which constituted a first valid lien upon the real estate located at 3451 East 149th Street, Cleveland, Ohio 44120. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "A" at [2). The Mortgage was filed for record on May 23, 2001 at Instrument No. 200105230040 of the Cuyahoga County Recorder's records and was subsequently assigned to Deutsche Bank. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "A" at [3). There was no dispute that Barksdale-Williams and Williams had defaulted under the terms of the Mortgage, thereby resulting in Deutsche Bank declaring the debt due and the Mortgage foreclosed. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "A", generally).
The docket in the prior foreclosure action reveals that the Summons and Complaint were served by Certified Mail and personal service. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). A
2 .-

process server certified that service was made by leaving a certified copy of the Summons and Complaint at the 3451 East 149th Street address. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). When the Certified Mail receipt was returned showing a failure of service on Barksdale-Williams as a result of the Summons being unclaimed, the Summons and Complaint were sent by Regular U.S. Mail to the 3451 East 149th Street address, pursuant to the Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Thereafter, on February 9, 2005, publication of the foreclosure was made. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B").
After proper notice, a default hearing was held and a default judgment was issued in Deutsche Bank's favor by the Magistrate on January 27, 2006. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). On March 2, 2006, the trial court adopted the Magistrate's decision and entered judgment for Appellee and against Barksdale-Williams and Williams "jointly and severally, in the sum of $68,050.86 with interest thereon at the rate of 9.25% per annum from 07/01/2004. Decree of foreclosure for Plaintiff". (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Thereafter, on May 4, 2006, the Court entered an Order providing notice of the foreclosure sale and approval of the appraisal fee and scheduling the foreclosure sale for June 5, 2006. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). The docket reflects that notice of the Sheriff's sale was published by Deutsche Bank on May 10, 2006. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B").
On May 12, 2006, Christopher Barksdale ("Appellant") filed a Motion for Relief from Judgment or Interim Stay of Foreclosure. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Appellant took issue with the conveyance of the property by Barksdale-Williams via a quit-claim deed executed on May 1, 2001. (R. a Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "C"). Specifically, Appellant argued that Williams caused a fraudulent conveyance. Appellant also argued that the trial court was without jurisdiction to sell the real property at foreclosure as a result of the filing of the
3

estate of Barksdale-Williams. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "C"). Appellant's own Motion, however, established that the Application for Authority to Administer Estate was not filed until April 21, 2006, more than one month after the entry of default judgment. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "C").
The Motion for Relief from Judgment or Interim Stay of Foreclosure was denied by the trial court on May 30, 2006. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Thereafter, Appellant filed an appeal with this Court. After briefing and oral argument, this Court issued its Journal Entry and Opinion on April 19, 2007, dismissing the appeal and ordering that a special mandate be sent to the trial court to carry the judgment into execution. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "D").
On April 24, 2007, Appellant filed a Motion for Reconsideration of this Court's decision. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). After the Motion for Reconsideration was fully briefed by the parties, the appellate court denied the Motion for Reconsideration on May 9, 2007. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Thereafter, on May 30, 2007, Deutsche Bank filed its Motion to Confirm the Sheriff's Sale, which had been held on June 5, 2006, but never confirmed, due to Appellant's appeal. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Appellant filed an Objection to the Motion to Confirm the Sheriff's Sale on the same day. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Over his objection, the trial court granted the Motion to Confirm the sale, issuing a decree of confirmation. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Appellant never appealed that Order. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). Instead, on December 31, 2007, he filed a Motion to Stay the Eviction in the original foreclosure action. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). That Motion to Stay was denied on January 2, 2008. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B").
In addition, Appellant filed the instant action, as a separate matter, on November 30, 2007, "as the sole beneficiary and as heir, devisee, executor or administrator of the Estate of
4

Jacqueline L. Barksdale-Williams", once again taking issue with the foreclosure action. Appellant attempted to serve the Summons and Complaint upon Appellee at two separate locations. The first address provided was Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas f/k/a Bankers Trust Company c/o Mortgage Lenders Network, 600 Wall Street, New York, New York 10005-0000. (R. at Docket). The second address was Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas f/k/a Bankers Trust Company, 120 East Fourth Street, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202-0000. (R. at Docket). Neither of these addresses, however, match Deutsche Bank's address as evidenced by the docket in the prior foreclosure action. (R. at Defendant's Response to Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment, Exhibit "A"). Rather, the foreclosure action, in which Plaintiff was an active participant, identified the proper address as Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas f/k/a Bankers Trust Company, as Trustee c/o Mortgage Lenders Network, 132 Welsh Road, Suite 100, Horsham, Pennsylvania 19044-0000. (R. at Defendant's Response to Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment, Exhibit "A"). Despite the fact that Appellant failed to serve Appellee at the correct address, Appellee entered an appearance by filing a Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment, on January 10, 2008.
On the same day, Appellant filed a Motion for Default Judgment, arguing that Defendant's Answer was due on or before January 9, 2008. (R. at Motion for Default Judgment). According to the docket, however, the Complaint was served at the New York address on December 10, 2007 and at the Cincinnati address on December 13, 2007, which would make the Answer dates January 7th and January 10th, respectively. Appellee's counsel never received a copy of the Summons and Complaint, which were served at the New York address. (R. at Defendant's Response to Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment, Exhibit "A"). Counsel did receive a copy of the Summons and Complaint served at the Cincinnati address
5

which was, in fact, the address of the attorneys handling the foreclosure matter. (R. at Defendant's Response to Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment, Exhibit "A").
Accordingly, because Appellee had knowledge of only the Complaint which was served on December 13, 2007, the Answer date was calculated as January 10, 2008, the date on which the Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment was filed. (R. at Defendant's Response to Plaintiff's Motion for Default Judgment, Exhibit "A"). The Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment was granted on January 30, 2008. It is from that Order that this appeal arises.
LAW AND ARGUMENT
A. Whether The Trial Court Abused Its Discretion In Denving Appellant's Motion for Default Judgment.
As set forth above, Appellee timely responded to the Complaint, filings its Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment on January 10, 2008. Even if the Trial Court had assumed that the Complaint served in New York on December 10, 2007 constituted proper service, which Appellee denies, it was still within the Trial Court's discretion to allow the filing of Defendant's Motion to Dismiss.
The Ohio Supreme Court has held that while Rule 12(A)(1) generally provides that a defendant must answer within twenty-eight (28) days after service of the Summons and Complaint, a Trial Court may, within its discretion, permit a tardy filing pursuant to Civ.R. 6(B)(2). Lindenschmidt v. Butler County Board of Commissioners (1995), 72 Ohio St.3d 464, 465. This Court has held that a trial court does not necessarily abuse its discretion when it permits a tardy filing, even if the party has not provided an explicit reason for delay, unless the other party is prejudiced by the delay. White v. Belcher, Cuyahoga App. No. 84214, 2004-Ohio-
6

5873, citing, Howland v. Lyons, Cuyahoga App. No. 77870, 2002-Ohio-982; Zimmerly v. Cleveland Clinic Foundation (July 30, 1998), Cuyahoga App. No. 73104.
As set forth above, Appellee provided an explanation to the Trial Court for the delay. Setting that aside, however, Appellant failed to even allege that he had in any way been prejudiced by the one-day delay in the filing of Defendant's Motion to Dismiss. In fact, Appellant responded to the Motion to Dismiss on January 14, 2008.
As noted by the Ohio Supreme Court, cases should be decided on their merits if possible, rather than on procedural grounds. Marion Prod. Credit Assn. v. Cochran (1988), 40 Ohio St.3d 265, 271. By allowing the filing of the Motion to Dismiss, the Trial Court allowed the matter to be decided on its merits, not on mere procedural grounds. As such, the Trial Court properly denied Appellant's Motion for Default Judgment.
B. Whether The Trial Court Erred In Granting Appellee's Motion To Dismiss Or, In The Alternative, Motion For Summary Judgment.
As set forth above, Appellant's Complaint in the instant action once again takes issue with the foreclosure action. Specifically, in the instant action, Appellant alleges that the quit- claim deed executed by Barksdale-Williams and the subsequent Mortgage executed by Barksdale-Williams and Williams are invalid and that Deutsche Bank's use of the instruments to initiate the foreclosure action is in some way improper. (R. at Complaint, Count One). Appellant further argues that he has suffered "economic loss of property" by the execution of the Note and Mortgage. (R. at Complaint, Count Two). Finally, Appellant appears to argue that he is entitled to possession of the real estate in question. (R. at Complaint, Count Three). These claims, however, are barred by the doctrine of res judicata as a result of the prior decisions, including that issued by this Court, in the original foreclosure action.
7 -

The Ohio Supreme Court has held that the doctrine of res judicata involves both claim preclusion and issue preclusion. Grava v. Parkman Twp. (1995), 73 Ohio St.3d 379, 381. Under the doctrine of res judicata, "a valid final judgment rendered upon the merits bars all subsequent actions based upon any claim arising out of the transaction or occurrence that was the subject matter of the previous action". (Emphasis added). Grava, supra, at syllabus. A transaction or occurrence has been defined as a "common nucleus of operative facts". Grava, supra, at 382, quoting, 1 Restatement of the Law 2d, Judgments (1982), 189-199, Section 24, Comment b.
The doctrine of res judicata requires a plaintiff to present every ground for relief in the first action. In Grava, the Ohio Supreme Court noted, "It has long been the law in Ohio that an existing final judgment or decree between the parties to litigation is conclusive as to all claims which were or might have been litigated in the first lawsuit ... the doctrine of res judicata requires a plaintiff to present every ground for relief in the first action, or be forever barred from asserting it". (Internal quotations and citations omitted). Grava, supra.
In the instant action, Appellant argues he was not a party to the original foreclosure action. In fact, however, Appellant was an active litigant in the foreclosure action. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "B"). In his Motion for Relief from Judgment or Interim Stay of Foreclosure, Appellant appeared as a "pro se heir of Jacqueline Barksdale-Williams". (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "C"). The appellate court found that Appellant lacked a present interest in the subject matter of the foreclosure litigation and, therefore, had not been prejudiced by the lower court's ruling. (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "D" at p. 4). The Court held "it is clear to this court that appellant cannot bring this action and recover in his own name. He owned no interest in the real estate and is not charged with possession of it. Therefore, it follows that he
8

had no authority to challenge the foreclosure sale". (R. at Motion to Dismiss, Exhibit "D" at p. 4). Accordingly, to the extent Appellant now seeks to challenge the foreclosure sale in his own name, he is barred by the appellate court's decision.
Likewise, to the extent Appellant seeks to challenge the foreclosure sale on behalf of the Estate of Barksdale-Williams, he is also barred by the doctrine of res judicata. At any time during the foreclosure action, Appellant could have entered an appearance as the administrator of his mother's estate. Yet, he failed to do so despite the fact that the Application for Authority to Administer Estate was not filed until April 21, 2006. The claims presented in the instant action could have and should have been litigated in the foreclosure action. Appellant's failure to do so bars him from litigating his claims now and his Complaint must be dismissed.
As set forth above, "the doctrine of res judicata requires a plaintiff to present every ground for relief in the first action or be forever barred from asserting it." (Emphasis added). Grava, supra. To the extent Appellant is seeking to bring claims on his own behalf, the appellate court has already held he does not have standing to do so. There can be no dispute that the prior decision of this Court was a valid final judgment rendered upon the merits. To the extent Appellant is seeking to assert claims on behalf of the Estate of Barksdale-Williams, those claims also could have, and should have, been asserted in the foreclosure action. The same transaction, i.e., the issuance of the Mortgage to Barksdale-Williams and Williams, is the subject matter of both the instant action and the foreclosure action. Clearly, both actions involve the same operative facts, as evidenced by the fact that Appellant himself attached to his Complaint in the instant action, pleadings and decisions from the foreclosure action. Appellant's failure to assert the claims he now attempts to bring in the foreclosure action bars him from litigating these claims now and therefore, the Trial Court properly dismissed his Complaint.
9

Moreover, the foreclosure action was filed in late 2004 with Appellant having been an active participant since May, 2006. To the extent that any issues concerning the foreclosure of the real property at issue exist, such claims could have, and should have, been brought in the foreclosure action. Appellant should not be allowed to forum shop simply because he did not receive the results to which he believes he was entitled in the foreclosure action. Moreover, Appellant fails to note that the Trial Court entered a Decree of Confirmation on October 17, 2007 in the foreclosure action. (R. at Opposition to Appellant's Motion for Stay of Execution, filed with this Court on February 21, 2008, at Exhibit "A"). That Decree of Confirmation was never appealed. Appellant cannot use the instant action as a means to circumvent the appeal process. Accordingly, the Decree of Confirmation must serve as a bar to the instant action as well.
CONCLUSION
Based upon the foregoing arguments and authorities, it is clear that the Trial Court did not err in either denying Appellant's Motion for Default Judgment or in granting Appellee's Motion to Dismiss or, in the Alternative, Motion for Summary Judgment. Accordingly, Appellee, Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas f/k/a Bankers Trust Company, as Trustee, respectfully requests that this Honorable Court affirm the judgment of the Trial Court.
10
